turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the first of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [warmly] Claire, what's on the table?
Three things. A month of quiet over the Strait of Hormuz ends in a single night of strikes.
Ooh. Heavy open.
Singapore moves to put a real age on the feed — thirteen, and the autoplay switched off for teenagers.
[curious] And the fun one?
Indonesia's malls have never been busier. The tills have never been quieter. And the country coined a word for it.
[chuckles] I love that already. Start with the strait.

So. The pause held about a month, and then it didn't. On Sunday, American forces struck two Revolutionary Guard rocket positions on Larak Island — that's the speck of Iranian land right inside the mouth of Hormuz.
Why there? Why that rock?
Central Command said the Guard was getting ready to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the shipping lane. First American strike on Iran since late July.
And Iran hit back.

Under a name — "Punishment of the Aggressor." Missiles and drones at two air bases in Jordan, which Amman says it intercepted, counting eight. And a claimed strike on a base in the United Arab Emirates.
[thoughtful] Claimed. You're doing the thing with your voice.
[wry] I am. Because the Emirates called that claim on itself — and I'm quoting — "baseless." They say they only intercepted drones over their own waters, and that nothing hit the base at all.
So somebody's overstating.
Which is the whole point of the sceptic's read. If Abu Dhabi is right, Tehran oversold the reach of its reply — and this is a contained tit-for-tat, not a widening war.
What did the market think? That's the tell, right?
Brent crude up about three per cent, to roughly ninety point nine dollars a barrel. Higher than it's been in weeks.
But not a spike.
[pause] Exactly. A market that genuinely believed Hormuz was closing would not stop at ninety-one dollars. The traders are pricing a violent punctuation, not a spiral.
Hold that thought about oil, because it walks straight into the money block.
It does. Because the bigger force this week isn't the strait — it's a man named Kevin Warsh.
The new Fed chair.
At Jackson Hole, he said, plainly, that inflation "is not beaten yet." And the market flipped.
Flipped how?
A month ago it priced the September meeting as a near-certain rate cut. Now it's a coin toss between a hold and a hike.
[exhales] From a cut to maybe a hike. That's a big mood swing.

And here's the signature of it. Gold and bitcoin fell together. Gold down about one per cent, near four thousand four hundred and forty-seven dollars. Bitcoin off about three per cent, near seventy-eight thousand four hundred.
Wait — they fell together? The two "debasement" trades, both down?
While the dollar firmed. And that's the tell of the week, Theo. When the anti-fiat assets sell off and the dollar rises, it's a rates story overpowering a fear story.
Higher-for-longer beats the geopolitics.

[thoughtful] For now. And notice what it does to the reader's own instruments. A firmer dollar and stubborn real yields are a headwind for gold and for bitcoin at once — which is why both are the week's casualties, despite exactly the kind of geopolitics that usually bids gold up.
So the fear trade lost to the rates trade. That's the sentence.

Global stocks held up — the all-world index near its record, around a hundred and ninety-five and a half. Singapore's index actually rose about one per cent, to five thousand seven hundred and fifty-five.
So equities shrugged.

For now. The vulnerability is exactly that oil loop — if the strait keeps Brent high and forces a September hike, equities are what gets tested next. And one honest note: the American jobs report isn't out until around the fifth. This is a regime read, not a data verdict.
Not investment advice, and Claire will glare at me if I forget it.
[deadpan] I'm glaring.
[laughs] Okay — Singapore. The age thing.
The Minister, Josephine Teo, set out the next step. A real minimum age of thirteen on six named platforms — Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, HardwareZone, X and YouTube.
Real age. Meaning not just typing in a birthday.

The Prime Minister's line was that self-declaration is "just not good enough." And for teenagers, the engagement features go off by default — autoplay, infinite scroll — plus a daily time limit a parent can set.
Honestly? As a design idea, going after the scroll and not just the door — that's the smart part.

The bill comes in twenty twenty-seven. But here's the sceptic, and it's a real one. Australia ran a world-first under-sixteen ban, and its own review found more than eight in ten under-sixteens still on the platforms three months later.
[skeptical] Eight in ten. So the line's easy to draw —
— and hard to hold. It comes down to the one thing nobody's solved: how you actually check an age without trading away everyone's privacy.
Speaking of the giants — the chip desk had a number this week that's hard to hold in your head.

Nvidia. Record quarter. Ninety-six point two billion dollars in three months, up a hundred and six per cent on the year. The data-centre part alone was eighty-nine billion — about ninety-two per cent of the company.
That's not a company, that's a weather system.
[wry] And the same week, its biggest customer showed up with a chip to bench against it. OpenAI, with Broadcom, detailed an inference chip called Jalapeño.
Jalapeño. [chuckles] Someone was hungry.

They claim one and a half to nearly twice the throughput per watt of Nvidia's outgoing part. But — those are the maker's own numbers, on the maker's own slide. Treat it as a vendor claim, not a verdict.
Still. When the guy renting all the shovels starts forging his own, that's a signal.
It is the one line item that dents the margin story — and it came, pointedly, from the company's single biggest customer. When the buyer starts building, the seller notices.
Down at our end of the rack — the home lab — the fun one this week is a number format.
The N V F P four format. Nvidia's Blackwell-native four-bit float — a way of shrinking a model that the reader's own card actually accelerates in hardware, instead of faking it.
Quantisation aimed at the exact chip on your desk. That's genuinely cool. Catch?
The N V F P four build is one uploader's work so far. So — a weekend experiment, not the workhorse, until someone independent checks the quality.
Fair. And the maker of the day — the Atelier — is my favourite kind of story. Belts.
[amused] Belts. And the whole desk is one sentence: everything that matters is visible at the cut edge.
Teach me. Thirty seconds.
Full-grain leather, one single strip, vegetable-tanned, solid brass buckle. Say those four back and you've read the belt.
And the price?

Here's the honest line. A sixty-dollar one-piece full-grain belt from a maker like Hanks — which carries a hundred-year warranty — is about ninety-five per cent of a three-hundred-dollar bespoke one, in durability.
So what's the last five per cent?

Fit and craft. Not more years. And the top of the market is where it gets funny. The Hermès buckle alone runs nine hundred to eleven hundred dollars, and Ferragamo's leather is widely called top-grain — not even the best grade. No designer buckle outlasts an eighty-nine-dollar Hanks. That's the logo tax, plainly.
[scoffs] Nine hundred dollars for a buckle. Okay. The kit desk — give me something I can actually buy today.
A ring. The Ultrahuman Ring Pro. Two-week battery, waterproof, and — the part that matters — no subscription. Everything's in the box, about three hundred and forty-nine dollars.
No monthly fee. In this category that's almost radical.

The buy-once reader should read the fee schedule before the sensor list. And the camera-free glasses we flagged back in issue eighty-seven — the RayNeo iO — finally go on sale on the fourth, at four hundred and seventy-nine dollars.
The ones with no camera. A little green screen in your eye.
A prompter and a translator you can wear all day. One correction — the "two days" battery was standby. Real translation is about six hours.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] And today it's a good one. Vinyl.
Records and turntables. And the number that surprises everyone: American vinyl earned one point four billion dollars in twenty twenty-four. Eighteen straight years of growth.
Eighteen years. The format the industry buried.
Forty-four million records sold, against thirty-three million CDs. Third year running it beat the CD on units.
So why does it hook people? Be honest. Is it the sound?

[thoughtful] Rarely, actually. The community's own honest answer is that it's the ritual. The sleeve in your hands. The one album you chose, start to finish. The forced attention that infinite shuffle quietly killed.
And when people insist it sounds better?
Usually it's a better master, not the format doing magic. Which brings us to the scandal that broke the word "analog."
Ooh. Tell me.
In twenty twenty-two, Mobile Fidelity — a premium label that sold records on an all-analog promise — admitted it had been using a digital step in the chain since twenty eleven.
[gasps] The "all-analog" label was secretly digital?
For eleven years. There was a class action. They settled for about twenty-five million dollars.
The label and the thing. Again. That's the whole issue, isn't it.

It is the spine. And if you want in, the honest starter path in Singapore is about a thousand to sixteen hundred dollars, all in — a proper entry deck, the cartridge it comes with, a phono stage, and a cleaning brush.
What's the one thing not to do?
[deadpan] The suitcase player. The cute little Crosley. The community says it tracks so heavy it shaves the groove — more damage in one play than three thousand on a good setup.
[laughs] So the cute one is the villain. Noted. And the money pit?

[wry] The cartridge ladder — each rung two to five times the last — and a three-thousand-six-hundred-dollar ultrasonic record cleaner. The hobby itself admits, when you press it, that most of the joy is ownership, not fidelity.
Okay, surfacing for air. Culture and the body — quick hits.
Venice. The film festival opens tomorrow with Danny Boyle's "Ink" — Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch.
Pearce as Murdoch. That I'll watch.
No reviews yet — nothing's screened. And the trade-press gripe is one woman among twenty directors in competition.
One of twenty. In twenty twenty-six. [sighs] Come on.
And a small redemption story closed out: Coyote versus Acme — the cartoon Warner shelved for a tax write-off — opened at fifteen and a half million dollars, on notices around ninety-five per cent.
The movie the studio tried to bury, and it's the best-reviewed of the bunch. Good.
On the audio shelf, Noble's new flagship headphone runs two kinds of driver at once — a dynamic and a planar-magnetic — in a wireless cup.
That used to need a cable and an amp. Endgame talk?
[deadpan] "Endgame" is a claim a headphone makes about itself. A measurement is what tells you it's true. We're waiting on the measurement.
The family desk — this one's close to home for the reader. Twelve-year-old daughter.
Secondary One. And the rules are arriving from two directions — the school-day phone ban that's already in force, and the age law taking shape for the feed at home.
What does the evidence actually say? Not the panic — the evidence.
A survey this year found twenty-five per cent of teenage girls say social media has hurt their mental health — against fourteen per cent of boys. The effect clusters in exactly her age band.
So it's real. But you've got a "but" face.

[thoughtful] The careful researchers — Candice Odgers, Andrew Przybylski — argue the causal evidence is thinner and more mixed than the headlines. Odgers warns a ban-first approach can get the problem wrong.
So the move is —
Phone out of the bedroom overnight. Watch what the screen replaces, not the raw hours. The tool buys you time; it doesn't raise the child.
[warmly] That's a good line. Fitness — I hear I'm supposed to walk with a heavy bag now.
Rucking. Walking under a loaded pack. It's the longevity crowd's efficient base — it keeps you in the aerobic zone while loading bone and posture.
And the number under it? What am I actually chasing?
V O two max. A study this year found each one-point gain in it lines up with roughly ten per cent lower mortality risk.
Ten per cent per point. Huh.
[wry] Though one coach's rebuttal is that they've rediscovered walking uphill. Which endurance coaches have prescribed for forty years.
[laughs] Rebranding the hill. Beautiful. Anything to book?
The Formula One night race, the ninth to eleventh of October — with its first-ever Sprint. And a restaurant: Assaggi, a Michelin-starred chef cooking a set lunch for fifty-eight dollars.
Fifty-eight for a starred hand. That's the value of the week.
[pause] And then the long read. Which is the whole issue in one image.
[curious] Go on.
Walk into a mall in Jakarta on a Saturday. Escalators packed. Food courts full. Queues for photographs.
Sounds like a boom.
Now look at what people are carrying. The hands are empty. And Indonesians noticed it before their economists did — so they made up a word. Rojali. It means, roughly, "the crowd that rarely buys."
[warmly] Oh, that's sharp. That's a little sad and very sharp.

There's a whole family of them now. The group that only asks. The group that only looks — or only strokes the merchandise. And it started as merchants mocking browsers, and got reclaimed. People say it about themselves now. "I'm proudly Rojali this month."
Because the official story says one thing —
— and the receipt says another. The government can announce five point two nine per cent growth, and be right. And the crowd can report that nobody they know is buying anything, and be right too.
How can both be true?

Because ten million people have fallen out of the middle class since twenty nineteen — and the growth number leans on government spending, not on shoppers. The university's own report called it "growth that disguises a weak economy."
So the mall visit is —

Dignity management. You keep the appearance of belonging — the mall visit, the coffee in the food court, the nice photo — while quietly refusing the middle-class purchase. The empty basket is a hedge against slipping down a rung, performed in public.
[thoughtful] And the deputy minister's line?
"Our shopping habits have changed, and there's nothing wrong with that." Which might even be half true. But — nobody memes a healthy economy into a mascot.
[thoughtful] No. They don't.
It's a folk index. Invented by ordinary people because the official ones stopped describing their lives. And when the official index and the folk one disagree, the folk one wins the culture.
Watch the folk indices. They're usually early.
[warmly] They usually are.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
